analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon emissions at $30 a ton, refunds low-income energy costs, and cuts the corporate tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action; it sat in two House committees until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a $30-per-metric-ton excise tax on carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels and large emitters, with the price rising 4% above inflation each year. It would send monthly energy refunds to low- and middle-income households to cover their higher energy bills, and fund a ten-year program of retraining, relocation, early retirement, and health benefits for displaced coal workers. It would also gradually cut the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 28%, add border adjustments so imports face the same carbon cost as domestic goods, and require Treasury to post the revenue's sources on a public website.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income households (under 200% of the poverty line, with the phaseout extending into the middle class) get monthly energy refunds sized to the estimated cost increase, delivered through SNAP-like channels with no withdrawal fees. Displaced coal workers get up to a decade of retraining, relocation, early-retirement, and health-benefit support funded by 2% of the bill's revenue. Renewable and low-carbon energy producers gain competitiveness as fossil fuels bear the tax. Corporations gain a lower income tax rate, stepping down from 35% to 28% after 2021. The public broadly benefits from reduced emissions, with refunds for fossil fuel capture and sequestration built in.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households, coal workers, clean energy, corporations

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $30-per-metric-ton tax on carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions from fossil fuel products and large emitters (25,000+ tons annually), rising 4% above inflation each year, with refunds for captured and permanently sequestered emissions.

Creates a Low-Income Energy Cost Mitigation Program providing monthly cash energy refunds to households at or below 200% of the poverty line, calibrated by the Energy Information Administration's estimate of the purchasing-power loss from the tax, with a phaseout designed to extend into middle-income households when revenue exceeds program costs.

Directs the Department of Labor to use up to 2% of the bill's revenue for ten years to assist coal workers displaced by the tax, through retraining, relocation expenses, early retirement, health benefits, and other aid.

Gradually reduces the corporate income tax rate to 32% in 2018 and 28% after 2021, and adds border adjustments so imported goods bear an equivalent carbon fee and exports can receive an equivalency refund.
Requires the Treasury Department to maintain a public website disclosing the amount and sources of revenue generated by the carbon tax.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and major emitters bear the excise tax, which would raise prices for gasoline, electricity, and other fossil-fuel-based goods. Households above the refund eligibility threshold face higher energy costs without full compensation. The Treasury gives up revenue from the corporate rate cut from 35% to 28%, partially offset by carbon tax revenue. Energy-intensive industries face higher input costs, softened only by export refunds and import fees that level the playing field.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and middle-to-upper-income energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The bill pairs the carbon tax with a permanent cut in the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 28%, a large revenue loss flowing to corporate shareholders that is only partly covered by the carbon tax revenue.

Households with incomes above 200% of the poverty line receive no energy refund and would bear the full increase in energy prices from the $30-per-ton tax, which hits transportation and home heating costs hardest for working and middle-class families.

The energy refund program is structurally complex: it relies on the Energy Information Administration to estimate annual purchasing-power losses, co-administers through state SNAP agencies with a multi-track eligibility web, and a revenue-sensitive phaseout formula that the Secretary must recalculate annually, creating administrative risk for a benefit low-income households would depend on.
Coal worker assistance is funded from only up to 2% of revenues for ten years, an amount that may fall short of the need in coal-dependent regions if the tax accelerates plant closures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and reasonably designed: a meaningful carbon price with refunds that fully compensate the lowest-income households for their energy bills, plus dedicated aid for coal workers, addresses the main fairness objection to carbon taxes. The serious drawback is the corporate rate cut, which hands a permanent tax reduction to corporations and shareholders as the political price for the carbon tax, narrowing the fiscal space the revenue could otherwise fund. Middle-income households just above the eligibility line are left exposed to higher energy costs.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2017 and referred to the Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce committees, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. John Delaney introduced the bill on April 6, 2017, joined by Reps. Matt Cartwright and Jared Polis as cosponsors, the only two cosponsors it attracted.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No further action was ever taken: the committees never reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor for a vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters came out ahead: they never faced the $30-per-ton carbon tax. Large corporations also kept the 35% corporate rate under this bill, though a separate 2017 tax law cut rates later that year. Low-income households and coal workers got no new energy refunds or transition assistance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax Pollution, Not Profits Act on April 6, 2017.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Kevin Brady)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup or reported the bill; it died in committee without action.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions within its jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded. All three supporters were Democrats in a Republican-controlled House, and the bill never advanced past committee referral, so no roll-call record shows where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers (oil, gas, and coal)
industries.note: The bill taxes their products' emissions at $30 per ton rising annually, directly cutting into their revenue on every barrel, ton, and cubic foot sold. Blocking the bill preserved the untaxed status quo, at the cost of continued unpriced carbon pollution the public bears.

Coal faces the heaviest carbon-tax exposure of any fuel, but the bill dedicates up to 2% of revenue for ten years to retrain, relocate, and provide health benefits to displaced coal workers, softening the blow for the workforce even as it accelerates the fuel's decline.

The bill cuts the corporate income rate from 35% to 28% after 2021, a permanent tax reduction for shareholders. It is the political counterweight that made the carbon tax package sellable to business, but the revenue forgone could otherwise fund public purposes.

A rising carbon price makes wind, solar, and other low-emission energy more cost-competitive against fossil fuels, and the bill pays refunds for capture and permanent sequestration that create a market for carbon management services.

They pay the carbon tax on their energy inputs, but border adjustments let exporters claim equivalency refunds and put matching fees on imports, protecting them from competing against goods produced without a carbon price.
